newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Sierra Leone to sign peace deal with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone to sign peace deal with rebels.

text.p: Sierra Leone's government and rebels are to sign a peace agreement on Saturday to end an almost forgotten civil war that has killed at least 10,000 people over five years.

Ivory Coast officials said on Friday the signing ceremony, attended by Sierra Leone President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh, would take place in the Ivorian commercial capital Abidjan, where the deal was agreed late on Thursday.
"This will be a celebration to which we have invited all the heads of state of the sub-region," one official said.
Host president Henri Konan Bedie and his government have spearheaded mediation efforts.
Sources close to the talks said Ivorian "perseverance" had brought the rebel delegation round to a conciliatory position.

Sankoh, whose Revolutionary United Front took up arms in 1991, had been in Ivory Coast since March but went to Sierra Leone last week to seek a mandate to sign from his fighters in the bush. He returned on Wednesday.

Traditional rulers from rebel-held areas in the east said Sankoh's fighters had demanded international monitors to guarantee their safety and disbanding of civil defence units made up of Kamajor traditional hunters before any signing.

The Kamajors had been attacking rebel positions across the nation and the truce extended by Tejan Kabbah and Sankoh in talks in Ivory Coast in April had looked more and more fragile until the latest peace developments.
Kabbah took office in March after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule. He had threatened to pursue the military option against the rebels if no deal was struck by December 1.
The rebels launched a low-level guerrilla campaign in the former British colony in March 1991. A 1992 army coup failed to end the war.
The war has been marked by atrocities including massacres of civilians and the hacking off of renegade soldiers' hands -- sometimes to intimidate would-be voters.
The rebels held 17 foreign hostages for months and disrupted the country's mainstay bauxite, rutile, diamonds and gold mining industry by forcing foreign-owned mines to close or cut back.
By early 1995 rebels were attacking close to the capital. The government brought in mercenaries from South African firm Executive Outcomes and retook the initiative.
Differences over the presence of Nigerian and Guinean troops and the South Africans had blocked a deal.
